# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–17 (Complete – Updated 132)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Spring of fifth year** (Chapter 17). Winter 1815-16 passed. Waterloo campaign: 16 June 1815 morning—regiment receives marching orders; afternoon/evening—cannonading; by 10 PM—Belgian hussar Regulus arrives with disaster tales; by dawn 17 June—wounded return; afternoon 17 June—victory news spreads; 18 June (Sunday)—religious services. **Critical event (26 March 1816)**: Rebecca delivers son and heir to Rawdon. **Spring 1816**: Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton (hastily arranged by Miss Crawley); they move into Miss Crawley's house. Lady Southdown assumes control. Miss Crawley dies (spring/early summer 1816). George Osborne's letter (written 16 June before dawn) delivered approximately three weeks after 18 June—early July 1815. **Late autumn 1815**: Mr. Osborne announces trip to Belgium; church incident with George's monument; confrontation with Colonel Dobbin in Brussels. **Chapter 17 timeline**: Approximately 3-4 years after Paris establishment; Rawdon and Rebecca now in Curzon Street, May Fair, London.
- **Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' hotel, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers, Curzon Street May Fair, Fulham, Park Lane), Brussels, Belgium, Waterloo battlefield, Brighton, Southampton, Paris, Faubourg St. Germain, Coldcombe hill farms, Dunholt, Calais, Dunkirk, Red Lion Square, Cursitor Street, Tooting, various other towns.

## Main Characters

**Captain William Dobbin (now Colonel)**
- **Promoted to Major, then Colonel** after second Major's death at Waterloo. Greatly respected as best officer and cleverest man. Secret, unrequited adoration of Amelia. Before campaign: instructed Jos to watch over Amelia. **Late autumn 1815**: In Brussels with recovering regiment. **Confrontation with Mr. Osborne**: Encountered Osborne in Brussels street; followed to Hotel du Parc; pleaded for forgiveness of Amelia and unborn child. **Osborne's refusal**: Complete rejection of reconciliation. **Dobbin's role**: Brought Amelia back to England to her mother's house in Fulham when Mrs. O'Dowd received summons. **Godfather to Georgy**: Became godfather of infant; purchases gifts constantly (cups, spoons, toys). **Chapter 17 status**: Visits Amelia's house daily for hours; visits Mr. Clapp's family regularly. Brings presents almost daily—recently wooden horse, drum, trumpet. Upon intimate moment with Amelia and child, experienced crushing realization of hopeless love. Knows there is no place for him in her heart despite her maternal affection. Gently bears his fate with fatal perspicuity; content to remain. Amelia laughs when he arrives, holds out hand, kisses him with "hopeless kindness." Her parents appear to encourage him without effect.

**George Osborne**
- **DEAD at Waterloo (16 June 1815, though monument inscription states 18 June)** — discrepancy noted. Married Amelia late April without father's consent; disinherited. Received £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. At Brussels: carried on desperate flirtation with Rebecca; sent letter and bouquet after campaign began. Departed 16 June with regiment. **Written final letter before daybreak 16 June** to father (delivered July via Dobbin's officer): farewell before great battle; imploration to provide for Amelia and possible child; contrition for irregularities; thanks; promise to act worthily. Letter sealed with sham coat of arms and "Pax in bello" motto. **The seal itself was robbed from George's dead body on battlefield**. **Monument erected** in church with Osborne arms, inscription stating death 18 June, aged 28, "while fighting for his king and country in the glorious victory of Waterloo. Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori." Depicts Britannia weeping over urn, broken sword, couchant lion.

**Amelia Osborne**
- **Widow and Mother**—George killed at Waterloo. Delivered infant Georgy (godchild to Colonel Dobbin), scarcely six months old. Status: receives £100/year widow's allowance; holds £2,000 in 4 percent annuities. **Health**: "Very bad" condition after Waterloo; "out of her mind like for six weeks or more"; life and reason "shaken by the blow." However, recovery underway by time Dobbin brought her to England. **Chapter 17 status**: Living with parents in Fulham; fully recovered and devoted entirely to mothering Georgy. Her existence is maternal caress; she envelops child with love and worship. Nurses, dresses, lives upon him; drove away all nurses; allows only her own hand to touch him. Considers allowing Dobbin occasionally to dandle him greatest favour. Shows bright maternal pleasure when infant's hands close round Dobbin's finger. Laughs when Major arrives; kisses him with hopeless kindness. Recovery complete.

**Captain Rawdon Crawley (now Colonel)**
- **Married to Rebecca**. Made last dispositions for Rebecca before campaign. Rode by General's side; gallantry mentioned in Gazette; promoted to Lieutenant-Colonel; awarded C.B. **Paris period (3-4 years post-Waterloo)**: Quitted Guards and sold out of army. Mustachios and title of Colonel only relics of military profession. Lived comfortably at Paris with Rebecca on "nothing per annum" for 2-3 years through undisclosed financial ingenuity. Owned skills in gambling and card games. **Gambling activities**: Regularly hosted card-tables at private evening reunions in Paris house. Played successfully with young officers (Green of Rifles, Blackstone of Hussars, Count Punter of Hanoverian Cavalry). **Incident with Colonel O'Dowd**: Loud violent fracas at Cafe de Paris; ladies engaged on both sides; Mrs. O'Dowd snapped fingers in Rebecca's face, called Rawdon "no betther than a black-leg"; Colonel Crawley challenged Colonel O'Dowd, C.B. Commander-in-Chief intervened (pistols "which he shot Captain Marker" were ready); no duel occurred. **Rebecca's intervention**: Went on knees to General Tufto; Crawley narrowly escaped being sent back to England; did not play except with civilians for some weeks after. **Recent assessment**: Rebecca convinced Rawdon that gambling as income was precarious; after few nights of suppers, gentlemen grew tired of play with him. **News of Miss Crawley's death**: Upon news aunt was dying, Colonel hastily departed Paris for Calais, then diverted to Dunkirk and Brussels (preferred Belgian city to noisy capitals; actually owed more money at London than Paris). **Current status (Chapter 17)**: Busy arranging affairs of inheritance in London; wife and child to follow; planning to take better lodgings; now occupying furnished house in Curzon Street, May Fair through arrangement allowing possession without payment.

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)**
- **Brussels post-departure**: Secured financial independence through horse sales to Jos, Rawdon's effects sales, stitched-away trinkets, bills, bank-notes. **Paris period (3-4 years post-Waterloop)**: Flourished in polite life; accommodates herself to fashionable life as if ancestors were people of fashion for centuries; merits place of honour in Vanity Fair through wit, talent, energy. **By 26 March 1816**: Delivered son and heir. Wrote all letters to Miss Crawley (attributed to Rawdon), sent war relics. **Miss Crawley's fury**: Made use of Miss Crawley's name to gain Parisian society entree. When discovered, Miss Crawley's fury "beyond bounds"; dictated furious answer to Briggs in English, repudiating Rebecca entirely as "most artful and dangerous person." Duchess of X (Parisian correspondent) did not understand English and reported to Rebecca that Miss Crawley sent "charming letter" with "benevolent things." **Parisian society success**: Achieved very smart and leading position; welcomed at distinguished houses of restored French nobility; English men of fashion courted her to disgust of their wives, who could not bear parvenue. **Son and heir**: After amiable fashion of French mothers, placed him out at nurse in village near Paris with numerous foster-brothers in wooden shoes. Father (Rawdon) would ride over to see him. Rebecca did not care much to visit; once infant spoiled dove-coloured pelisse; preferred nurse's caresses to mamma's. Child almost drowned on Calais sands during mother's absence when French maid Mademoiselle Genevieve neglected charge to pursue soldier from Calais garrison. **Chapter 17 journey and creditor negotiations**: Upon news of Miss Crawley's death, ordered intense mourning. Departed Paris in landlord's carriage with French bonne and child. **Creditor negotiations (COMPLETED)**: Negotiated with creditors (chief: Mr. Davids of Red Lion Square, Mr. Manasseh of Cursitor Street) representing Colonel's debts. Did not employ lawyer; used creditors' own lawyers (Mr. Lewis, Mr. Moss) who complimented her business brilliance. Offered creditors ninepence or shilling per pound dividend, securing Rawdon's return to England. Negotiated creditors down through fifteen hundred pounds ready money to cover debts exceeding fifteen thousand pounds, purchasing more than ten times that amount of debts. Treated lawyers to sherry and bread cake at lodgings; returned to Continent to rejoin husband and report "entire liberation." **London society (Chapter 17)**: Speedily became vogue among certain class; demure chariots at her door with great people; carriage in park surrounded by dandies; opera box crowded with constantly changing heads; wit, cleverness, flippancy made her fashionable. **Female society rejection**: Ladies hold aloof; doors shut. Few female acquaintances from abroad declined to visit; cut her severely in public. Lady Bareacres gathered daughters protectively at opera; Lady de la Mole (who rode with Becky at Brussels) did not recognize her in Hyde Park. Mrs. Blenkinsop cut her at church. Rebecca now attends church regularly with Rawdon, carrying gilt prayer-books, performing ceremony with grave resignation. **Current residence**: Occupies furnished house in Curzon Street, May Fair, without payment through landlord arrangement.

**Mr. Raggles (Former Butler)**
- **Background**: Born on family estate of Queen's Crawley; younger son of gardener. Through good conduct, handsome person and calves, grave demeanour, rose from knife-board to footboard to butler's pantry. Served Miss Crawley many years with good wages, fat perquisites, opportunity to save. **Marriage**: Contracted matrimonial alliance with late cook of Miss Crawley's who subsisted by exercise of mangle and keeping small greengrocer's shop in neighbourhood. Marriage clandestinely performed years before; news brought to Miss Crawley by children of seven and eight years. **Property acquisition and current status (Chapter 17)**: Purchased house in Curzon Street to let to tenants; intended to subside into greengrocer's shop once tenant found. **Current prosperity**: House brings handsome yearly income; footer occasionally lounges at area railing treated with respect; cook takes green stuff from his shop and calls him Mr. Landlord; tenants unaware of landlord's knowledge of every household activity and meal. Good man, good and happy. Sends children to good schools (Charles to Dr. Swishtail's boarding at Sugar-cane Lodge; Matilda to Miss Peckover's, Laurentinum House, Clapham). **Devotion to Crawley family**: Loves and adores as author of prosperity; maintains silhouette of Miss Crawley in back shop; drawing of Porter's Lodge at Queen's Crawley done by spinster in India ink; only addition to Curzon Street House decorations is print of Queen's Crawley in Hampshire, seat of Sir Walpole Crawley, Baronet, represented in gilded car drawn by six white horses, passing lake with swans and barges containing ladies and musicians. Believes no palace compares to Queen's Crawley, no family more august. **Current tenant (Crawley/Rawdon)**: Craiwleys are current tenants in furnished house.

**Raggles' Financial Relationship with Rawdons (Chapter 17 - Critical Detail)**
- Rawdon and Rebecca generously give patronage to Miss Crawley's tradesmen and purveyors; some willing, especially poor ones. Washerwoman from Tooting brings cart weekly with bills week after week. Raggles himself supplies greengroceries. **Nobody paid**: Not blacksmith who opened lock; glazier who mended pane; jobber who let carriage; groom who drove it; butcher; coals; cook; servants who ate. Every servant owed greater part of wages, kept up perforce interest in house. Bills remain outstanding for servants' porter at Fortune of War public house (described as "curiosity in chronicles of beer"). This is narrated as example of how people "live elegantly on nothing a year."

**Other Characters**
- **Mr. Osborne (Elder)**: George's father in Russell Square. Placed household in mourning; cancelled parties; closed house front. Made no communication to Mr. Bullock (future son-in-law). **Late autumn 1815**: Announced trip to Belgium. **In Brussels**: Visited hotel garden; sought soldiers from --th regiment; paid guinea to wounded convalescent to bring Sergeant to Hotel du Parc. **Confrontation with Dobbin**: Dobbin pleaded for forgiveness of Amelia and child. **Osborne's response**: Broke into rhapsody of self-praise and imprecations, swore never to recognize Amelia as George's wife or speak to her, stated he was "a man of his word" and would "stick to to the last day of my life." Complete refusal of reconciliation. Soldiers feasted on generosity from his "proud purse of mourning."
- **Mrs. O'Dowd**: Spent five hours by Amelia's side during cannonading; distinguished herself at Waterloo; Major became Colonel and C.B.; received peremptory summons forcing her to quit Amelia; confronted Rebecca at Cafe de Paris.
- **Sir William Dobbin (Alderman)**: Called upon Mr. Osborne senior approximately three weeks after 18 June with pale, agitated face; delivered George's sealed letter.
- **Jos Sedley**: Fled Brussels 16 June toward Ghent road on horseback with Isidor, abandoning Amelia and company. Mrs. O'Dowd made scornful remarks. Current status (late autumn 1815): Widow Amelia's available source of financial aid, though willingness uncertain.
- **Other established characters**: Osborne's Sisters, Mr. Clapp, Little Mary (Clapp's daughter), Tom Stubble, Pauline, Isidor, Towzer, Sergeant, James Crawley (Jim), General Tufto, Mrs. Brent, Lieutenant Spooney, Blackstone, Count Punter, Green (Rifles), Colonel O'Dowd, Lady Southdown, Pitt Crawley, Lady Jane Crawley, Briggs, Bowls, Firkin, Creamer, Rodgers, Mr. Waxy (solicitor), Creamer (dismissed physician), Mademoiselle Genevieve (French bonne), Orrin Stenworth, Cotho Hollwood, Marie Lindson (RUMOR - possibly dead of plague per peddler report via Orrin). **Rumor**: Marie Lindson dead of plague (unverified rumor started by Orrin, heard from peddler).

## Critical Facts and Status
- **George's Monument Discrepancy**: Inscription states 18 June 1815; actual death 16 June 1815.
- **Amelia's Complete Recovery**: Fully recovered, devoted entirely to mothering Georgy in Fulham with parents.
- **Dobbin's Hopeless Love**: Recognizes fatal perspicuity that no place for him in Amelia's heart, entirely absorbed in motherhood.
- **Rebecca's London Reception**: Fashionable among certain class; ladies and society doors shut to her; cut publicly by former friends and acquaintances.
- **Rawdons' Financial Operation**: Live in furnished Curzon Street house without payment through landlord (Raggles) arrangement; accumulate substantial unpaid debts to tradesmen while maintaining fashionable appearance—pattern exemplifying "living elegantly on nothing a year."
- **Raggles' Prosperity and Vulnerability**: Prosperously landlord to Crawley tenants; his income entirely dependent on their occupancy and eventual payment; unwitting victim of systematic credit exploitation.
